i4.body:
## Root cause

The provisioning skip checks a Python environment below the SDK even though the workspace creates that environment at the repository root. A provisioned checkout therefore repeats environment synchronization instead of using its existing installation.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Developers provisioning onetaskgraph worktrees.
**What it costs them.** Each provisioning call repeats a synchronization that should be skipped and can unnecessarily reach the package index.
**What it costs the product owner.** Provisioning has recurring avoidable work; no current timing or extra spend estimate establishes a larger slowdown.
**Cost of the workaround.** There is no acceptable workaround: There is no supported way to make the incorrect existence check recognize the actual workspace environment without changing provisioning or inventing a second environment.

- Severity: medium
- Workaround: none
- Severity with the workaround: medium
- Priority estimate: high (severity with the workaround medium; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently)

## Examples

The recorded worktree had the CLI in its root environment while the SDK-local environment did not exist.

## Suggested fix

Check the environment at the uv workspace root on each platform before deciding whether synchronization is needed.

**Contributing locations.**
- onetaskgraph `scripts/provision-gate.sh`: tests for an SDK-local interpreter while syncing a workspace member.
- onetaskgraph `pyproject.toml`: declares the Python SDK as a member of the repository-root uv workspace.

### onetaskgraph — `onetaskgraph`

Provisioning skips environment synchronization once the workspace-root interpreter exists on Unix or Windows. No CLI interface changes.

i7.title: onepipeline: Bootstrap fixtures must isolate their prerequisite tool state
i7.body:
## Root cause

A bootstrap verification fixture should control the tools already installed before it tests provisioning a missing tracer. Instead it relies on a tool installed in the real checkout while rejecting the installation a clean checkout legitimately needs. The provisioning journey fails on a clean setup for a reason unrelated to tracer provisioning, and an already populated checkout masks it.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Developers running the Linux bootstrap provisioning journey on clean checkouts.

**What it costs them.** The successful CI-bootstrap case fails before completing its intended assertions whenever the pinned plan-store binary is absent.

**What it costs the product owner.** Clean-checkout verification produces a false failure and loses useful provisioning coverage. The run reproduced it with both original and changed bootstrap recipes; no production bootstrap failure was shown.

**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: Install the pinned prerequisite with the ordinary bootstrap once per checkout before running this test.
- Side effects on the outcome: None to the product; the fixture still depends on the host’s installed state.
- Discovery: The failure names the cargo install request, making the missing prerequisite apparent.

- Severity: medium
- Workaround: Provision the pinned plan-store prerequisite once through normal bootstrap before running the journey.
- Severity with the workaround: low
- Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 5 occurrences; raised one level because it fires consistently and it has 3 or more occurrences)

## Examples

The run’s focused provisioning suite reported three passing journeys and this failing journey; restoring the original bootstrap reproduced the failure. The basis still accepts only cargo fetch in the fixture double while normal bootstrap may install the plan store.

## Suggested fix

Make the fixture provide its own preinstalled plan-store prerequisite at the path the bootstrap reads, and direct the bootstrap’s tool root into that fixture. Keep the double refusing unplanned installs so the journey measures tracer provisioning independently of the real checkout.

**Contributing locations.**
- onepipeline `tests/provisioning.rs`: constructs a cargo double that rejects installs without controlling the plan-store installation root.
- onepipeline `justfile`: the bootstrap reads the pinned tool from a checkout-owned root instead of a fixture-selectable root.

### Provisioning recipe — `onepipeline` (`justfile`)

Allow an explicit tool root for callers that need isolated provisioning; the default remains the current checkout tool root.

```diff
+ONEPIPELINE_TOOLS_ROOT=<directory>  # optional; overrides the bootstrap tool root
```

### Bootstrap journey — `onepipeline` (`tests/provisioning.rs`)

Use that root inside the fixture and preinstall the other prerequisite there before testing tracer absence, refusal and installation. No additional public interface changes.

## Owning runs

- prepush-gate-only-without-ci-2

## Evidence

Verification ran on host lima-hp.

i9.title: ai-orchestrator: Hiding one test tool must preserve the other tools on PATH
i9.body:
## Root cause

The isolated session journeys hide one tool by moving its directory's other commands behind every remaining search directory. That changes which unrelated tools the session runs. On this host the real installer is displaced by a version-manager shim whose configuration the isolated session does not have, so provisioning proofs fail before they can exercise installation.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Developers running session provisioning proofs on hosts with both direct tools and version-manager shims.

**What it costs them.** Both missing-tool and moved-tool-directory journeys fail reproducibly when the replacement installer cannot run in their private home.

**What it costs the product owner.** Required provisioning proofs block delivery in this host configuration despite the real installer being available; this is a situational development block.

**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: Select a search path with the direct installer available and no competing version-manager shim before running the suite.
- Side effects on the outcome: None; the journeys still run the real installer into their private tool directories.
- Discovery: A maintainer must inspect captured setup stderr; the failed assertion itself prints only an empty command result.

- Severity: high
- Workaround: Run the provisioning proofs with the real installer resolving ahead of version-manager shims after tool filtering.
- Severity with the workaround: low
- Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently)

## Examples

Both provisioning journeys failed in a fresh verification at this basis. A diagnostic probe of the moved-directory case captured “No version is set for command uv”, followed by the logged installer failure. Setup then continued as its optional-tool policy specifies, and the proof could not resolve the tool it intended to install.

## Suggested fix

Preserve the original lookup precedence of every retained executable when hiding selected tools: replace a removed search directory with its filtered sibling directory at the same position, rather than appending retained commands at the end. The isolated session then runs the same installer it inspected before replacing its home.

**Contributing locations.**
- ai-orchestrator `tests/session_setup/test_locked_plan_store_setup_e2e.py:495`: filters directories containing a missing tool and appends all retained executables at the end, changing their precedence.
- ai-orchestrator `tests/session_setup/test_locked_plan_store_setup_e2e.py:550`: resolves installer directories before changing the home, then uses the reordered search path in the isolated home.

### Session provisioning journeys — `github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator`

A session hiding named tools continues to resolve every other command to the executable that won before filtering. This changes fixture behavior without changing a public CLI.

## Owning runs

- npm-engine-install

## Related tickets

- [ai-orchestrator: PATH fixtures must preserve one entry even when its target is missing](https://github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator/issues/2004) — related: Both fixes preserve retained command identities while filtering the test search path, but dangling-link deduplication and precedence require independent corrections.

## Evidence

Host: U-17UN402ICR95C. Basis: github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator at 816b71455aae578cf9133e78ef7d67033a7b1c77.

i16.body: ## Root cause The required Linux pull-request gate injects the repository's `GH_PROJECTS_TOKEN` into live GitHub Projects tests and requires that credentialed tier to pass. This happens only while the allowance is exhausted (2 recorded). **What it costs the product owner.** By the rate-allowance ruling this is judged on the work it stops. The development area decides: merging is blocked for up to an hour at a time, intermittently. i1.title: dero-skills: Tier lint must accept independently selected test directories
i1.body:
## Root cause

The Python tier rule accepts only a separate project, even when a separate directory and build target already keep slow tests out of the fast target. Correctly isolated integration suites are repeatedly flagged and need suppressions.

## Impact

The panic said `expected "must be a resolved commit id" in exit status: 1`: the script exited non-zero, but Nx's captured stdout/stderr did not include the script's own refusal text. ## Suggested fix The original suggested change is retained below; no additional remedy is inferred. **Contributing locations.** - github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs `scripts/nx.sh`: Named in the original text reproduced below. ### Suggested change — `github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs` When `scripts/nx.sh` streams (`ONEVCS_NX_SHOW_OUTPUT=1`), it runs targets with Nx's streamed output style, so a target's own stdout and stderr pass straight through rather than being captured and replayed. For a deferred publication adopting an existing draft, push the new branch head even when its tree equals the base, preserving the draft and returning an unchecked result without opening a new change request.

i7.title: onevcs: Callers must be able to require a moved base at session open
i7.body:
## Root cause

A caller that needs a draft physically restacked cannot require a session open to merge the moved base. Repository policy may skip a clean merge, so the caller must perform its own merge to guarantee the draft contains the base.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Developers and operators using onevcs in the conditions described above.

**What it costs them.** Library consumers implementing stack readjustment must duplicate merge orchestration to guarantee placement.

**What it costs the product owner.** Library consumers implementing stack readjustment must duplicate merge orchestration to guarantee placement. No monthly dollar cost or provider subscription-quota share is established by this evidence.

**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: One explicit recovery step per occurrence by the affected developer or manager: Perform the required base merge in the consumer after session opening.
- Side effects on the outcome: The intended outcome is retained; verification or delivery requires an extra manual step.
- Discovery: The draft records the recovery, but the normal workflow does not reliably direct the user to it; identifying it takes inspection of the failure and these instructions.

- Severity: medium
- Workaround: Perform the required base merge in the consumer after session opening.
- Severity with the workaround: low
- Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently)

## Examples

Library consumers implementing stack readjustment must duplicate merge orchestration to guarantee placement.

## Suggested fix

Add a per-open requirement to merge the moved base, overriding the repository’s conditional policy for that open, and let the engine adopt it instead of merging the base itself.

**Contributing locations.**
- github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs `crates/onevcs/src/base_merge.rs`: The conditional policy can skip a clean merge.
- github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs `crates/onevcs/src/workspace.rs`: Session opening has no caller requirement to force that merge.

### onevcs — `github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs`

Add a per-open requirement to merge the moved base, overriding the repository’s conditional policy for that open, and let the engine adopt it instead of merging the base itself. The documented behavior changes as stated above.

The session-open request gains a requirement rather than a second repository policy. True forces the base merge at this open; false keeps the configured policy. The CLI exposes the same requirement.

i8.title: ai-orchestrator: Revised plans do not select their current visual evidence
i8.body: ## Root cause When a plan is revised after its visual spike has finished, the design document should show the replacement visual evidence the revision produced. The planning flow always reads the original canonical report instead, so a separately named second visual report is omitted and the design document retains the earlier pictures unless the planner manually replaces the canonical report. ## Impact **Who is affected.** Planners and people reviewing a revised plan with a second visual spike. **What it costs them.** Every separately named replacement report is ignored by the design writer. Reviewers can judge the revised design against obsolete pictures; the recorded revision required an explicit handoff to avoid that outcome. **What it costs the product owner.** Revised visual plans risk approval against obsolete evidence. This is a real risk to planning quality, rather than a demonstrated outage or loss of work; no measured workflow slowdown or extra spend is claimed. **Cost of the workaround.** - Applying it: The planner instructs the replacement spike to regenerate the canonical report from its new answers and images, once per revision. - Side effects on the outcome: The current design receives the right images; the canonical report no longer preserves the earlier version. - Discovery: The planner must discover which report the planning tail reads; the recorded planner raised a manager question to establish the handoff. - Severity: medium - Workaround: Have the replacement spike regenerate the canonical visual report before finishing the revised plan. - Severity with the workaround: low - Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently) ## Examples This run revised a plan after its first visual spike had settled. Its planner needed a second visual spike and arranged for it to regenerate the canonical report, because letting it write only its own report would leave the rewritten design document showing the old images. ## Suggested fix Record the report chosen as the current visual evidence on the plan, and have both design composition and visual approval resolve that selection. A revision updates only the affected portions of the existing visual changes document, preserving unchanged decisions, descriptions and image assets, and explicitly selects the resulting current report. Preserve earlier report versions while ensuring the writer receives the current report's answers and images. Resolve copied reports through their provenance, so the selection works with either current report naming or plan-qualified report naming. **Contributing locations.** - github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator `orchestrator/spike_plan.py`: selects only the reserved canonical report; the visual convention allows one reserved visual spike per plan. - github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator `scripts/finish-plan.sh`: quotes only that selected report's answers and assets into the design writer's task. - github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator `orchestrator/design_approval.py`: relies on the same canonical selection when determining whether visual evidence must be shown. ### Visual evidence convention — `github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator` The plan explicitly names its active visual report. Revision replaces this selection, and all visual evidence readers resolve it consistently; an unresolved selection refuses finishing or approving the plan instead of silently selecting old evidence. Existing plans without a selection retain the canonical-report default. ```yaml metadata: orchestrator.visual-report: "" ``` Revising the visual changes document is incremental: use the existing document as the baseline, update only sections and image assets affected by the revision, and retain all unaffected content. If a separately named report is produced, it carries the complete current evidence, including unchanged content from that baseline, rather than only the revision's delta. Selecting a different report does not require recreating the document or regenerating unchanged visuals. The selected report's visual changes and image assets are the ones quoted into the design document. Existing CLI invocation forms remain unchanged. ## Owning runs - manager-landings-supervised-revise ## Related tickets - [ai-orchestrator: spike report ids collide across plans in a flat document source](https://github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator/issues/1557) — related: Plan-qualified report names prevent collisions between plans but independently leave revisions needing to select their current visual evidence. ## Evidence Verification host: lima-hp. Repository basis: github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator at 219568e3c890b5521b7ed7a75868355a21c5e950, recorded after fetching origin/main. Draft: drafts:manager-landings-supervised-revise/drafts/20261013T101138Z-ai-orchestrator-the-plan-flow-reads-one-canonica; run manager-landings-supervised-revise; author manager, no node. The manager draft has no transcript command. Its occurrence records planner question correlation c-7e32f0821e47bcdf6aed0df1f18e9405 and the canonical-report regeneration handoff. At the recorded basis, the report selector compares report names only with the reserved canonical report, and the finishing recipe passes only that report's answers and images to the writer. Source references are the contributing locations above, at lines 326–340 and 666–675 respectively; the approval reader uses the same selection at line 924. Verification establishes the selection mechanism; the reported handoff comes from the manager's occurrence record. Historical Duplicate search: Queries: "visual report"; "visual spike"; "spike-visual-report"; "spike_plan.py". - [onepipeline: Required visual context conflicts with the advisory guide](https://github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline/issues/821): Reconciling merge-check guidance does not select a revised plan's current evidence. - [onetaskgraph: Unused partial source overlays reject every store command](https://github.com/nickderobertis/onetaskgraph/issues/3574): Validating only selected sources does not change which visual report a plan reads. - [ai-orchestrator: spike report ids collide across plans in a flat document source](https://github.com/nickderobertis/ai-orchestrator/issues/1557): Namespacing reports prevents cross-plan collisions but does not select a replacement report within one revised plan; its accepted fix leaves this cause unchanged.

i9.title: onevcs: An ordinary session-branch push must pass through managed publication
i9.body:
## Root cause

A dispatched worker can push its managed session branch directly even though delivery requires the lifecycle’s publication operation. The push reaches the host without the session’s publication record, so supervision must discover it after the fact and ask the worker to publish again.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Managers and workers delivering changes from managed session worktrees.
**What it costs them.** Three workers bypassed managed publication in this run and needed corrective notes and republication to restore lifecycle evidence.
**What it costs the product owner.** Delivery bookkeeping and supervision can diverge from the actual remote branch, creating a recurring output-quality risk.
**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: Run onevcs publish for the same session and wait for its managed closeout.
- Side effects on the outcome: none; the intended result is retained.
- Discovery: The dispatch appendix explicitly names the publication route, but a raw push succeeds without a diagnostic directing the worker back to it.

- Severity: medium
- Workaround: Republish the existing session through the managed publication verb.
- Severity with the workaround: low
- Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently)

## Examples

The monitor caught raw branch pushes in the non-e2e cost, live-suite and figures delivery nodes after they had reached the remote.

## Suggested fix

Install a managed-session pre-push guard that requires the current lifecycle publication context, and have the publication operation establish that context only for its own push while preserving the repository’s existing hook.

**Contributing locations.**
- onevcs `crates/onevcs/src/workspace.rs`: creates managed worktrees whose ordinary pushes are not restricted to the lifecycle publication operation.
- onevcs `crates/onevcs/src/publish.rs`: must supply the session-bound publication context consumed by the guard.

### onevcs — `onevcs`

An ordinary raw push from a managed session is refused before reaching the remote and names onevcs publish <session> as the remedy. Managed publication still runs the repository’s own hook; this is protection against accidental bypass, not an adversarial credential boundary.

## Owning runs

## Evidence

Verified on shulgin at 341a8a0012ba3463333b6b92b47fca1749faece8.
The three manager-recorded monitor findings name raw push commands and remote heads. The basis publication lifecycle has no session-bound pre-push routing guard.

A loaded runner can correctly record a refused publication and still fail the required check because scheduling consumes the fixed tolerance. ## Impact **Who is affected.** Developers landing onevcs changes. **What it costs them.** An intermittent required-check failure forces another gate run; the reported release waited about nine hours. **What it costs the product owner.** Some release and contribution checks stop on runner scheduling rather than a product defect.

Preserve assertions that a refused gate is recorded failed and that its elapsed duration matches its own timestamps. This changes test behavior without changing a public interface. ## Evidence The November 10 release check failed its timestamp comparison while 456 of 457 tests in that partition passed; an earlier attempt on the same tree passed. i12.title: onepipeline-ui: release-plz semver pass can enable bundled UI without its build
i12.body: ## Root cause `the implementation detailed below` runs the repository semver gate, while `the implementation detailed below` still enables release-plz’s independent semver reading. That second command can infer `bundled-ui` without a built UI and misread the failed build as compatibility. ## Impact **Who is affected.** Maintainers reviewing onepipeline-ui release pull requests, and consumers reading its changelog. **What it costs them.** release-plz's own semver reading builds the crate with `bundled-ui` but without the built UI, fails, and reports the failure as API compatible. A release pull request can then carry no report of a real API break, though the repository's own `just semver-check` step still rules on compatibility. This happens on every release run. **What it costs the product owner.** Original assessment: The development area decides: the release review's break report is unreliable, a real risk to output quality, while the repository gate still refuses a release that claims compatibility over a break. That is `medium`. **Cost of the workaround.** - Applying it: read the `just semver-check` step's output in the release workflow during review, a minute per release. - Side effects on the outcome: none. - Discovery: mostly free. The release workflow runs that step by name immediately before opening the pull request. - Severity: medium - Workaround: inspect `just semver-check` output during release review - Severity with the workaround: low - Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently) ## Examples The worker reproduced a cargo-semver-checks build failure without the UI dist while the repository script reached a break verdict. ## Suggested fix The original suggested change is retained below; no additional remedy is inferred. **Contributing locations.** - github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui `.github/workflows/release-plz.yml`: Named in the original text reproduced below. - github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui `release-plz.toml`: Named in the original text reproduced below. `.github/workflows/release-plz.yml:122` runs the repository semver gate, while `release-plz.toml` still enables release-plz’s independent semver reading. i13.title: onepipeline-ui: Merge CI omits the breaking engine-pin announcement check
i13.body:
## Root cause

Pull-request gates must reject an unannounced incompatible engine requirement before merge.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Maintainers and agents releasing onepipeline-ui, and the downstream runs waiting to adopt its next release.

**What it costs them.** The pull-request checks never run the semver announcement check, so an engine pin crossing a semver boundary under a non-breaking subject merges green. release-plz then refuses every release until a separate breaking announcement lands, and dependents wait on it. This happens every time such a pin move merges unannounced (1 recorded).

**What it costs the product owner.** the release workflow is blocked after such a merge, which follows a regularly made kind of change but only when its subject omits the break. That is a situational block, so `high`.

**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: land a separate pull request carrying the breaking announcement, one change request's gate and merge, then let release-plz retry.
- Side effects on the outcome: the release, and any adoption waiting on it, is delayed by that extra change.
- Discovery: free. The release-side refusal names the engine requirement and says to announce it.

- Severity: high
- Workaround: Land a separate explicit breaking announcement, then let release-plz retry against the corrected commit range.
- Severity with the workaround: medium
- Priority estimate: high (severity with the workaround medium; fires consistently; 5 occurrences; raised one level because it fires consistently and it has 3 or more occurrences)

## Examples

PR #160’s pin move required the later #163 announcement. PR #170 moved =0.55.0 to =0.56.0 under a non-breaking subject, and release-plz failed both immediately and after #169, holding aio-adopt-history-fix until another announcement.

## Suggested fix

Run the semver announcement check on every pull request against the last release's baseline, reading the proposed squash subject as the announcement, and make it a required check. An unannounced incompatible engine pin is then refused before merge instead of blocking the release after it. The release-side check stays as the final safeguard.

**Contributing locations.**
- github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: runs the ordinary quality gates but does not invoke semver-check against the last release baseline. `.github/workflows/release-plz.yml:131-133` runs that check only after landing. `scripts/semver-check.sh:157-260` treats an engine requirement crossing its semver boundary without a breaking commit announcement as a refusal. Thus the omission permits changes that deterministically fail release validation after merge.

### Pull-request CI — `onepipeline-ui` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```diff
 required pull-request checks: <existing quality gates>
+required pull-request check: semver announcement (just semver-check against the last release baseline, the PR title read as the squash subject)
```

i14.title: onepipeline: Changes to shipped release inputs must trigger a release
i14.body:
## Root cause

Changes to packaging and release tooling can change what users install without triggering a release. Consumers waiting for the changed distribution then wait until an unrelated packaged-code change releases it.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Maintainers and downstream consumers of packaging-only changes.

**What it costs them.** A merged distribution change remains unavailable and its dependent adoption waits indefinitely.

**What it costs the product owner.** Some release adoptions cannot finish without a separate release-triggering intervention.

**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: The manager must diagnose the missing release and prepare one small additional change.
- Side effects on the outcome: Delivery or verification waits; the intended result is preserved.
- Discovery: The draft and its recorded failure identify the affected workflow, but a maintainer must read that evidence to identify this workaround.

- Severity: high
- Workaround: Arrange a release by making an intentional packaged release-note change that announces the pending distribution change.
- Severity with the workaround: low
- Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently)

## Examples

A merged distribution change remains unavailable and its dependent adoption waits indefinitely.

## Suggested fix

Make release eligibility include every input that changes a published artifact, independently of the crate archive inclusion list. Preserve conventional-commit classification while ensuring a packaging-only eligible commit creates a version-bump proposal.

**Contributing locations.**
- onepipeline `release-plz.toml:6`: limits release detection to packaged inputs.
- onepipeline `Cargo.toml:1332`: excludes packaging and release scripts from the archive input set.
- onepipeline `.github/workflows/release-plz.yml:127`: runs release discovery without including those omitted distribution changes.

### onepipeline — `github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline`

Release eligibility includes npm packaging and release tooling changes even when no crate-packaged source changes. The registry artifact layout is unchanged.

## Owning runs

- npm-engine-install

i19.body: ## Root cause The published-adoption release hold identifies a dependency to onevcs by landing commit even when several pieces of work share that commit; onevcs rejects the ambiguous reference. ## Impact **Who is affected.** Managers running plans whose nodes adopt a dependency `published`, when that dependency's landing commit is shared by several pieces of work, as when stacked branches land together. **What it costs them.** The hold asks onevcs about the dependency by its landing commit, onevcs refuses the commit as ambiguous, and the hold answers "not answered" for as long as the run lasts, even after the release is out. The node never launches on its own; the observed hold re-surfaced for over four hours after publication. This happens every time such a dependency is asked about. **What it costs the product owner.** Original assessment: The users area decides: release-held adoption, the mechanism these plans depend on to land, fails in that situation and stalls the dependent work indefinitely, so `high`. **Cost of the workaround.** - Applying it: confirm the release on the registry, then flip the held node to `fast` adoption by live edit, a few minutes of a manager's time. - Side effects on the outcome: the node adopts under the weaker mode, without the engine confirming the release it consumes. - Discovery: partly free. The recurring wait surface says the hold is unanswered and the manager's options include flipping it to `fast`, but nothing says the release is already out. - Severity: high - Workaround: confirm the release on the registry, then flip the held node to fast adoption by live edit - Severity with the workaround: medium - Priority estimate: high (severity with the workaround medium; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently) ## Examples Three dependency branches shared landing commits and release-wait kept answering not-answered after crate and PyPI 0.51.0 published. ## Suggested fix The original suggested change is retained below; no additional remedy is inferred. **Contributing locations.** - github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline `not stated in old text`: The old text does not state this. ### Suggested change — `github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline` onevcs types its ambiguous-reference refusal, and the release hold falls back to the dependency's preserved change-request URL on that refusal as it already does on an unresolvable one. The URL names one piece of work, so the hold gets an answer and releases when the dependency's release is out. #### Release status refusals — `onevcs` ```diff Error::UnresolvableReference { reference } +Error::AmbiguousReference { reference, candidates } # several pieces of work answer to one reference ``` #### Release hold — `onepipeline` ```diff -ask at the landing commit; on UnresolvableReference ask again at the change-request URL +ask at the landing commit; on UnresolvableReference or AmbiguousReference ask again at the change-request URL ``` ## Rejected fixes Preserving a separate branch-name reference and adding another fallback was rejected because https://github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline/issues/420 already preserves the change-request URL and provides the fallback path. i21.title: onevcs: Recovery must validate object stores only when the selected work needs them
i21.body:
## Root cause

A recovery query should pay object-store validation only for answers it will use. It eagerly lists and proves store contents even when the selected launcher has no owed rows, adding cold-read CPU and repeated warm-read filesystem work.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Developers and managers using onevcs.

**What it costs them.** The no-row cold read used 5–7% more CPU than the baseline; store listing and proving contributed 0.35–0.8 seconds of summed thread time.

**What it costs the product owner.** The affected workflow incurs recurring friction or loses reliable evidence about its result. The recorded evidence does not establish a dollar or subscription-quota loss.

**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: Use the existing timeout-bounded Git fallback for queries where proving a store cannot save work. This adds a manual step for the person supervising the affected occurrence.
- Side effects on the outcome: no intended work is lost, but verification or supervision is delayed.
- Discovery: the error does not name this workaround; checking the recorded symptom and applying the diagnosed response takes a few minutes of a developer’s time.

- Severity: medium
- Workaround: Use the existing timeout-bounded Git fallback for queries where proving a store cannot save work.
- Severity with the workaround: low
- Priority estimate: medium (severity with the workaround low; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently)

## Examples

The no-row cold read used 5–7% more CPU than the baseline; store listing and proving contributed 0.35–0.8 seconds of summed thread time.

## Suggested fix

Defer store integrity admission until a selected in-process object answer needs it, and share the admitted generation within that query; preserve damaged-in-place invalidation for every answer actually used.

**Contributing locations.**
- github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs `crates/onevcs/src/recovery_cache.rs`: lists and proves stores eagerly as part of the query context.
- github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs `crates/onevcs/src/vcs.rs`: opens store contexts while scanning selected identities even when no resulting row needs an in-process answer.

### onevcs — `github.com/nickderobertis/onevcs`

Defer store integrity admission until a selected in-process object answer needs it, and share the admitted generation within that query; preserve damaged-in-place invalidation for every answer actually used.

The documented behaviour changes as stated above; existing command forms and output schemas otherwise remain unchanged.

i22.title: onevcs: Warm recovery must reuse immutable derivations within its latency budget
i22.body:
## Root cause

Repeated recovery decisions should reuse immutable repository answers while checking that their store context is still valid. Rebuilding commit graphs and repeating the same immutable derivations leaves the tenfold warm workload above its declared latency budget.

## Impact

**Who is affected.** Developers and managers using onevcs.

**What it costs them.** Tenfold warm calls took 475–965 milliseconds against a 300-millisecond budget; each call reopened about 11,000 loose objects.

**What it costs the product owner.** The affected workflow incurs recurring friction or loses reliable evidence about its result. The recorded evidence does not establish a dollar or subscription-quota loss.

**Cost of the workaround.**
- Applying it: Run latency-budget verification on the quiet CI runner while retaining the full correctness workload. This adds a manual step for the person supervising the affected occurrence.
- Side effects on the outcome: no intended work is lost, but verification or supervision is delayed.
- Discovery: the error does not name this workaround; checking the recorded symptom and applying the diagnosed response takes a few minutes of a developer’s time.

- Severity: medium
- Workaround: Run latency-budget verification on the quiet CI runner while retaining the full correctness workload.
- Severity with the workaround: low
- Priority estimate: low (severity with the workaround low; fires intermittently; 1 occurrence; not raised)

Keep a bounded process-local cache of immutable commit, ancestry and diff answers keyed by source store and the existing integrity context; reuse those answers across recovery calls and discard them when that context changes.

i23.title: onetaskgraph: Local updates respect a task made read-only
i23.body:
## Root cause Updating a local task replaces its file even when a person made that file read-only. The update bypasses the refusal that protects other local writes, so a deliberate protection against rewriting is ignored. ## Impact **Who is affected.** People protecting local task files and callers issuing status or metadata updates. **What it costs them.** An update can change a protected ticket and report success. **What it costs the product owner.** User intent is violated and protected task content can be replaced by an otherwise routine update.
Cost of the workaround - Workaround: Remove write permission from the containing directory while the task must be protected. - Applying it: A person adjusts directory permissions for the protected interval. - Side effects on the outcome: All ticket updates in that directory are blocked, making this unsuitable for shared active folders. - Discovery: The update reports success; source inspection is needed to discover why file permissions were insufficient.
Priority calculation - Severity: high - Severity with the workaround: medium - Priority estimate: high (severity with the workaround medium; fires consistently; 1 occurrence; raised one level because it fires consistently)
## Examples A grooming journey made a task read-only and still observed a successful status and metadata update. ## Suggested fix
Contributing locations - onetaskgraph `crates/onetaskgraph-local-md/src/lib.rs`: updates through atomic replacement without a writability check. - onetaskgraph `crates/onetaskgraph-local-md/src/lib.rs`: checks writability on one write path while replacement omits it.
### onetaskgraph — `onetaskgraph` Require an existing task file to be writable before staging every atomic replacement, including metadata-only and status updates. Preserve its existing permissions and return the existing per-item unavailable error without staging or changing content when it is not writable. This changes refusal behavior without changing the public interface. ## Evidence The run observed a successful update of a read-only local task. The verified update path calls replacement directly; the writability check exists only in the other atomic-write entry point.
